name: Name
title: DEAD ON\nARRIVAL
body: By Matthew D. Wilson

name: Name
body:
Dawn broke over the Marchfells, a thick brume blanketing the marshlands as the first rays of sunlight began to warm the air. Major Anson Wolfe squinted through the light reflecting off the placid water as he scanned the opposite bank from his vantage on the western edge of the Black River. It was a vast waterway, even this narrow stretch before him, wide and deep enough to allow the passage of all but the largest maritime vessels. Within the clinging mist, he could just make out the silhouettes of several figures.
"How many do you reckon?" Wolfe asked, scratching at his graying beard. The gorget of his heavy warcaster armor was fitted too tightly to his chin, so his whiskers continually snagged in the metal seams, a constant annoyance he’d been intending to have the Legion’s mechaniks correct. But the major’s busy days left little time for personal maintenance.
The willowy man on his right peered through a small brass spyglass, chewing his lip in concentration. After counting by way of a few muffled grunts, he finally produced an answer. "Twenty…maybe thirty. Hard to say when they won’t stand still. Definitely Iosans…. Well, maybe Skorne? Pretty sure Iosans. Some big fellas among them, though." He paused, pressing the spyglass even tighter to his eye. "Iosans. They’ve got myrmidons. I can see the glow."

name: Name
body:
"Myrmidons?" came a nasally voice over Wolfe’s left shoulder.
"Iosan warjacks," Wolfe said, wondering if his tone sounded more dismissive than he had intended. His patience for the baron’s presence had worn thin long before the major had arrived with his platoon of legionnaires that morning.
"Why don’t they just call them warjacks?" the baron said. Had the man not been the cousin of Wolfe’s lifelong friend, Duke Alain Runewood—once the lord of the duchy this stretch of river bordered—he would have instructed him to keep his claptrap shut. Fortunately, Preston Marse was quicker to answer.
"Look here." Marse handed the spyglass to the baron, who raised it to his eye. "They might look like warjacks—same number of legs, arms and a head, all where you’d expect ’em to be. But under the hood, they’re as different from warjacks as you are from the elves that built them."
Marse was a field agent of the Cygnaran Reconnaissance Service. Information was his stock and trade, and there was nothing he liked better than to impress others with it—a trait Wolfe often thought risky for someone in the intelligence service, but one he was happy to employ to his advantage all the same.

name: Name
body:
"The power source for myrmidons works on completely different principles than common steamjacks or warjacks. They’ve got arcane workings, as opposed to any practical sort of fuel-burning engine. You might think they’re similar to these new electrified ’jacks the major’s Storm Legion is using here," Marse wagged a thumb in Wolfe’s direction, "but you’d be wrong as a razorbat thinking that. Even these storm-things have some basic science inside them. But the myrmidons, they’re as magical as magic gets while still being held together with nuts and bolts. Ages ahead of our own tech and able to twist and bend energy in ways you can’t even imagine unless you’ve seen it with your own eyes. And we ain’t really never understood how."
Baron Caldwell handed the spyglass back to Marse, any interest he might have had evaporating when presented with information that might require the unthinkable effort of consideration. "Can you get them to leave or not?"
The storm chamber powering Wolfe’s custom-made armor hummed as he paced aimlessly along the riverbank. He needed to put a little distance between himself and Caldwell. Deep-seated resentment toward the aristocracy predisposed Wolfe to resist any direction that might be satisfying to the baron. "Technically, they are outside the borders of Cygnar, Lord Caldwell. We’ve no right to ask them to move on."

name: Name
body: Caldwell wrinkled his nose. "I wasn’t thinking so much you’d ask as you’d use all these knights at your disposal to give them a reason to scurry back to their forest." "The Storm Legion are not knights." Wolfe smiled tightly, his teeth clenched. He had been instrumental in founding the new Storm Legion after Cygnar had disbanded the former Storm Knights, a class-based branch of Cygnar’s military service that catered to the nobility. "And they are not in service of Cygnar’s nobility." Entitlement is one of the hardest traits to put down, he thought as he turned to face the baron. "We’re here because the CRS has expressed concerns." The baron puffed his chest out, straining the buttons on his fine jacquard vest. "The Reconnaissance Service would not know of the presence of these elves had I not sent word." Marse stepped between the baron and Wolfe. "Indeed. And that’s what has made this particularly interesting, Lord Caldwell. We haven’t seen hide nor hair of the Iosans since the last days of the Infernal War. We weren’t even sure if there were any of them left. You know how damned secluded their nation is." He waved his hand vaguely in the air as if to punctuate his statement. "There’s been no word for nearly a decade; we’ve heard nothing but rumors and vague reports of some unspoken tragedy. But them showing up like this, and most peculiarly, in this spot—as far south as they can be without crossing a border of Cygnar or the Protectorate. And just sitting. It’s got heads being scratched all the way back to Caspia."

name: Name
body: "It’s disruptive, is what it is," Caldwell replied, continuing as if Marse hadn’t spoken. "Word travels, you know. And trade along the King’s Highway has stalled because of it. That means less toll revenue, a fact I’m sure the Crown would be concerned with. Something must be done." Caldwell left no room for disagreement. How quickly they settle back into their old ways, Wolfe thought. It hadn’t been so long ago that the whole of humanity teetered on the brink of annihilation. Otherworldly demonic forces had waged war against the Iron Kingdoms to reconcile a debt of souls owed in exchange for bestowing the Gift of Magic on man four centuries past. For Wolfe, the wounds suffered during a barely-averted apocalypse had yet to mend. But to the nobility of Cygnar, the most pressing concern was lost toll road revenue. Once again, it was Wolfe’s job to help avert catastrophe. Try as he might, he couldn’t suppress the deep, guttural growl that welled up inside him. "I’ll see to it." ***

name: Name
body:
Wolfe tested the small rowboat, an loan from a local river trapper, by tentatively placing one foot within its leaky hull. It creaked, protesting the weight of his armor, but it held together, much to his surprise. The arcane turbine in his warcaster armor produced an anti-gravitational field that buoyed its weight, making something that should have been far too heavy for any normal person not only wearable but capable of assisting him in combat. But that was while on dry land, and Wolfe was unsure how the arcane physics of the powered suit would act on the water. But even more concerning, whereas the steam-powered armor of the last generation would simply see their boilers extinguished when submerged in water, Wolfe had no idea how the lightning-charged power plant of his new armor would react to submersion, and he wasn’t keen to find out, regardless of how much electrical insulation surrounded him.
"Surely you could send a messenger across more easily," said Preston Marse, just as skeptical as Wolfe was that the rowboat provided a sound means of crossing the river. Behind Marse , the hulking Stryker warjack Wolfe nicknamed Bingo buzzed in agreement. Another Stryker, dubbed The General in honor of the famous namesake of this model, rattled its legendary sword upon its shield, aggressively volunteering for the job. The entire Storm Legion platoon had assembled on the riverbank, and no one seemed at ease with the idea of Wolfe taking it upon himself to confront the unknown presence on the other side of the Black River.

name: Name
body:
"We don’t know if they’re hostile," Wolfe said, rocking the boat back and forth to see if anything might shake loose.
"Then we send a rider to King’s Vine. We can have a barge here within a day that could ferry half the platoon and your ’jacks, too." Marse’s concern was genuine, but anyone who knew the major also knew he wouldn’t send someone into a situation he wouldn’t go into himself. Some among his superiors viewed this as a shortcoming, a weakness in his leadership ability, his inability to prioritize resources. Those that served under him felt differently.
"Another day of lost revenue," Baron Caldwell thought out loud.
"Let’s just get this over with," Wolfe said, the baron entirely unaware of his steely glare. He stepped completely into the dingy and sat down on the bench. The boat creaked loudly under his weight, sinking several inches.
Marse hitched up his long coat to keep it free of the water as he stepped into the boat and took a seat at its stern. "Well, if you’re going to insist, then you’re not going alone. I want a look up close at these peculiar Iosans."

name: Name
body:
Wolfe opened his mouth to protest but was caught off guard as the baron followed behind Marse, climbing onto the bow of the tiny boat. "Someone needs to be present to represent the interests of the Crown," Caldwell said, adjusting his starched collar as he took his seat at the helm.
"Really, that’s not necessary, Baron," Wolfe started, unsure of whether to be put off by Caldwell’s presence or impressed by the lack of timidity his kind was generally known for.
"Get us underway, Major. This whole affair has gone on long enough," Caldwell said.
Wolfe bristled but otherwise ignored the baron, instead addressing his lieutenant standing ready on the riverbank.
"Put three sharpshooters in cover along the bank. If I raise my hand up," he said, straightening his arm above him, "remove whatever targets you can make."
Lieutenant Pierce nodded her head. "Yes sir."
Without a moment’s delay, she barked orders that sent the platoon’s sharpshooters searching for the optimal locations to cover his crossing.
Bingo lurched forward, rocking the boat as his mechanical foot stomped into the river.

name: Name
body:
"No room left in the boat, pal," Wolfe said out loud though unnecessarily, as he could command the warjack with thought alone. Bingo objected with an electric crackle, and Wolfe raised his palm. "I know you’ve got my back."
The warjack stepped to the side, brandishing the heavy mag-bolter that comprised its left arm. The weapon was capable of propelling a massive slug at long range, and Bingo’s aim was unmatched. Wolfe nodded at the warjack, silently confirming its orders as he put the oars of the rowboat into the water and pushed off from the riverbank.
Wolfe looked up at Marse, perched on the end of the rowboat, his bird-like gaze fixed on the opposite shore. "Wasn’t expecting this to be a tour cruise."
Marse combed his fingers through his black hair, smiling. "Good thing you have that fancy armor to get the job done. Little good these hands would be if it were the other way around."
Wolfe chuckled at the comment, but the subtext was not lost on him. His biggest fear right now was somehow ending up in the water. But when it came to combat, Wolfe was far better equipped than the CRS agent, unarmored and with nothing but a single-shot forgelock pistol at his side. If they were headed toward a confrontation, Wolfe was the only one of the three who had a fighting chance. His mechanika-powered armor was an advantage beyond compare and not just when it came to rowing a boat. He was also a trained warrior and a warcaster, equipped with an arsenal of arcane spells as well as a cohort of warjacks, at least one of which was watching over him with a long-range magnetic projectile accelerator that could put a hole through two inches of solid steel.

name: Name
body:
His thoughts were interrupted by Caldwell. "How long do you suppose this should take, Major?"
"I could drop you off right here if you’re in a hurry," Wolfe growled as he continued to row them across the Black River.
Caldwell gulped as he looked around, for the first time possibly realizing he had rushed headlong into a situation that was quite literally over his head.
The remainder of the crossing went without conversation, which said something for Marse, who rarely allowed silence to persist. Wolfe stared down at the water pooling at his feet, seeping in through cracks in the boat’s slats, and hoped the tiny craft would get them safely to the other side.
As the mid-morning sun burned off the fog, the mysterious assembly on the eastern bank came into view.
"These are not the Iosans we knew," Marse whispered as if afraid his voice might carry across the water.
Wolfe strained in his armor to get a look behind him, his back toward their destined shore. "How do you mean?"
Marse slowly shook his head, slack-jawed. "They are…different…"

name: Name
body:
Wolfe silently cursed his decision to row the boat, unable to clearly view the assembly he was headed toward. But his arcane senses prickled as he closed on the easter riverbank. Another warcaster was nearby.
Along the shore, the figures began to move. Four myrmidons advanced to the edge of the riverbank. Two massive constructs clad in burnished steel and armed with shields and long, deadly swords took center, flanked by a pair of smaller myrmidons, equipped with hooked halberds and shields. Beside the myrmidons, ranks of black-eyed elven soldiers formed, some with their hands on the hilts of their sheathed long swords, others with rifles held across their chests. They were what the Iosans called "soulless"—elves born without an immortal soul, little more than empty vessels that existed to do the bidding of their masters. Wolfe had seen them in the employ of the now-disbanded Retribution of Scyrah forces, and while chilling to behold at first, they were not in any other way physically dissimilar to their souled brethren. But it was the line of more heavily armored soldiers that towered above them, brandishing massive compound bows as tall as a man, that caused Wolfe to feel he might have rushed into the unknown too hastily. What little flesh could be seen beneath their dark cowls was ashen white and desiccated like that of a corpse, and their grim expressions simmered with quiet rage. They were not the elven kind Wolfe knew, at least not anymore.

name: Name
body:
"Major, I fear I have made a mistake." Marse’s voice quivered. "I’m a spy, not a fighter, and I must say, I do my best work from afar. Perhaps we should reconsider —"
"Turn this boat around this instant," the baron demanded, the panic in his voice evident despite his attempt to speak as quietly as possible. "Get us out of here before it is too late."
If the Iosans couldn’t hear them before, Wolfe was sure the crescendo the baron’s voice rose to had certainly traveled the dozen meters between the boat and the shore. He angled the prow of the boat slightly so he could have a better view of their welcoming party as he closed on the riverbank.
"Let’s just stay calm," he said. So far, none of the soldiers along the bank had raised a weapon to indicate a threat. If the Iosans wanted them dead, they could have sunk the tiny craft at any time. But the baron clearly took no comfort in this, and Wolfe knew his panic could quickly turn into a liability.
"This was a grave miscalculation, Major." Caldwell’s hoarse voice shook as he spoke. "This is nothing short of a trap."

name: Name
body:
"I don’t think it’s a trap." Wolfe, still rowing, hoped he sounded more certain of himself than he felt. Another stroke of the oars carried them a boat length closer.
"What’s this?" the baron started, his voice now shrill.
Wolfe managed to twist his head over his shoulder enough to see a figure emerge from between the two towering myrmidons. Though not as tall as the archers, she was no less imposing. Clad in intricately crafted armor, inlaid with mesmerizing channels that glowed with arcane energy from within, and a helm fitted with multiple luminescent optical nodes, she had the appearance of a mechanical wasp, and the twin-bladed magelocks held at her sides only underscored her inherent deadliness. This was the warcaster he had sensed.
His face aghast, Marse jumped slightly from his seat, reaching toward the baron. "Baron, I wouldn’t —"
"Send the signal, Wolfe!" The baron rose on unsteady legs, looking back to the west bank as he thrust his arm into the air. "Signal your shooters!"
Wolfe’s mind pulsed as he sensed Bingo responding to the baron’s attempt to signal the sharpshooters. In the span of a heartbeat, rifles raised and arrows were nocked within the Iosan ranks.

name: Name
body:
"No!" Wolfe cried out, as much in response to Bingo as to the baron as he unconsciously commanded the warjack to stand down. The boat rocked under Wolfe’s weight as he whirled around to grab Caldwell’s arm, but the sudden movement pitched the unstable baron overboard, just yards from shore. Wolfe fell onto his chest over the prow of the rowboat, his armored fist searching below the surface of the dark water until it found the baron and hoisted him up by the collar, sputtering and gasping for breath.
As the rowboat drifted the last few feet to the riverbank, Wolfe raised his head to look directly at the Iosan warcaster. Those around her had raised weapons defensively, yet she had not so much as twitched. He was simultaneously grateful for her steadfast calm and  filled with apprehension about what exactly he had gotten himself into.
***

name: Name
body:
Wolfe made no attempt to salvage any semblance of dignity. After an awkward dismount from the rowboat that brought him up to his chest in river water, silently thanking Morrow that he had not been electrocuted while in the following breath wishing to Thamar that the baron had, he stood before the Iosan warcaster. He held his hands out at his sides in as welcoming a gesture as he could manage given his mud-filled boots and waterlogged gambeson.
"That’s not exactly how I imagined that going," he said, forcing a chuckle.
The Iosan warcaster holstered her pistols and took two paces down the sloping riverbank toward him. Even through his armor, he felt the air around him chill as she drew near. His skin prickled, and a shiver ran down his spine—he knew he was in the presence of undeath.
When she spoke, it was like the rustling of leaves, a rasp as she forced the air consciously from her chest in an effort to produce the sound of a voice. "What did you…imagine…exactly?"
Even in her coarse voice, Wolfe could hear the lilting tongue of her Iosan accent. She spoke Cygnaran well, but her words were measured with the careful pauses of one who had not spoken the language in a very long time.

name: Name
body:
"I just meant—" Wolfe found himself suddenly tongue-tied, his faculties rattled by the searing gaze of the warcaster’s glowing optics so close to his face. He clenched his teeth to prevent them from chattering due to the icy chill that burrowed into his flesh. Unconsciously, he stepped back, his foot sinking into the muddy shoreline.
"I should have preferred to make a more formal introduction for my companions and myself." He gestured to the dripping-wet baron shivering beside him and to Marse, who had not yet found his way out of the rowboat.
The warcaster’s elongated helm twitched as her gaze moved from Wolfe to the baron, to Marse, and back to Wolfe again. Her movements were unnatural, intentionally, almost mechanically, precise.
"Proceed," she said, the central glowing orb of her helm locking with his eyes.
Wolfe cleared his throat to buy himself a moment to navigate the awkward discourse unfolding. Formalities were not his strength. "I am Major Anson Wolfe, commander of the First Infantry Battalion of the Cygnaran Storm Legion. The man in the boat is my colleague, an agent of Cygnar’s Reconnaissance Service.

name: Name
body: And this," he said, clapping the baron on the back with a wet thwack that sent the man staggering forward ever so slightly, "is Baron Abercrombie Caldwell, Lord Consul of the Cygnaran Duchy of the Eastern Midlunds. It was at his behest that we have come to inquire about your intentions." The baron tensed, grumbling through clenched teeth at Wolfe. "You said it was because of CRS concerns." "He represents the interests of the Crown," Wolfe added with an overtly grandiose tone, grinning widely as he nudged the baron forward. Arms clasped around his soaked velvet coat, the baron fumbled for words as the warcaster cocked her head in his direction. "It’s just…it’s been a few days," he stammered, "We would just like to know what you— who you…are, and what you’re doing here?" The warcaster stepped toward the baron and scanned her surroundings with a series of slight, twitching head movements before focusing her luminous gaze directly on his face. With the advantage of the embankment’s slope, she stood a full head and shoulders taller than the baron, but she would have towered over him even on level ground.

name: Name
body:
"Here? This…place? Land…that no sovereign power…holds…claim over?" Her deathly pale lips, the only flesh visible beneath her helm, pursed as she appeared to wait motionless for the baron’s reply.
Caldwell’s knees shook. "Um…yes."
The warcaster strode back up the embankment to join the ranks of her soldiers, then turned to address the three Cygnarans with the consummate delivery of a highborn patrician artfully skilled in the ceremonies of royal statesmanship.
"I am Hellyth, Scyir of Nightfall, Arms Master to House Kallyss, Preeminent Chamber of the High Convocation of the Empire of the Eternal Dusk." She paused for a shallow bow before continuing. "We have been…awaiting an ambassador of Cygnar…so we might…request safe passage to your nation’s capital."
Comforted by Hellyth’s seemingly benign request, Preston Marse crept out of the boat to stand just behind Wolfe’s left shoulder. "You could have made this a little less distressing if you’d raised a white flag or something."
Hellyth cocked her head toward him. "White…flag?"

name: Name
body:
He shrank a bit behind Wolfe. "A symbol for peaceful intent, you know?"
She paused, considering this for a moment, then said, "We have…no such thing."
Tired of standing in the muck, Wolfe tromped up the muddy bank. "People get nervous when a war party camps on their doorstep. This is a lot of hardware to travel with if you’re just being neighborly."
"The…myrmidons? Our…soldiers?" Wolfe would have sworn he heard her chuckle. "My apologies for any…confusion. We do not need to protect ourselves…from Cygnarans."
Wolfe wasn’t sure if that was a subtle insult, a challenge, or if something was being lost in translation, but he didn’t want to take the time to unpack it. "Either way, you’ve got our attention now. Why do you want passage to Caspia?"
Instead of answering, Hellyth turned and hissed a command to her soldiers in her native tongue. The soulless warriors and the towering archers clapped their weapons in reply as they assembled in two rows behind Hellyth’s myrmidons, facing each other to form a corridor that led beneath a thick copse of shadowy willow trees.

name: Name
body:
"Please." She beckoned the three men to follow her within.
"I’ll just wait with the boat," Caldwell whispered to Wolfe, shuffling in the opposite direction.
"Alone?" Wolfe said without looking back, following the Iosan warcaster into the processional tunnel of myrmidons and soldiers.
The baron cast a glance at the empty, leaky rowboat, then reconsidered and followed behind Marse and the major.
The soulless stared forward with empty, expressionless black eyes. They stood at attention, as unnaturally still as the undead in their midst, though they were nonetheless alive and breathing. As he got a closer look at the archers, however, Wolfe determined they appeared corpse-like in every way other than the fact they were standing upright.
"You are not Iosan," Wolfe probed.
"Iosan is…who we were," Hellyth replied flatly.
Wolfe took a moment to choose his words. "Then, who are you now?"
Hellyth stopped and turned to face Wolfe. She cocked her head unnervingly. "Who? Or what?"
Slowly, Wolfe nodded.
"We are Dusk," Hellyth said. "We are eldritch."

name: Name
body:
"Eldritch?"
"As the moment that exists between the light of day and the dark of night," she rasped, "so do we."
The Scyir of Nightfall turned and continued to lead them into the shadows ahead. After another dozen yards, they emerged beneath the boughs of several great willow trees, where the area had been cleared to create a secluded camp sparsely equipped with traveling kit and provisions. Softly glowing lanterns illuminated the space; at the center sat a robed figure upon a small pile of cushions.
Hellyth raised a hand, indicating that Wolfe, Marse, and Caldwell should wait near the edge of the clearing. She walked on to stand beside the hooded figure, and Wolfe could barely hear a short exchange in their language. After a moment, the figure rose. Gangly beneath flowing white robes, it walked toward Wolfe with stiff, awkward strides. Nearly eight feet tall, the creature towered over him as it drew back its hood. Long, white strands of hair fell from a withered skull, its eyes so sunken they would have been invisible save for a soft, amber glow—the only lifelike aspect of the macabre, desiccated, and twisted being that stood before the three men.

name: Name
body: "Thank you for your audience," the eldritch wheezed, every word grating against a larynx as dry as parchment. "I am Vynyshill, High Seeker of the late Consulate Court, counsel to House Kallyss, Preeminent Chamber of the High Convocation of the Empire of the Eternal Dusk." She paused, drawing air into the dry lungs within her emaciated chest. "We have come to pay our last respects to your king."
